scoreNote: Strong (5): a recommendation-appropriate response that names the circumstances in which early training helps and those in which early selection harms, and qualifies the policy accordingly; concrete examples and a clear stance.

sentences.text: It is natural to want to nurture exceptional talent, and starting early can seem the obvious way to turn promise into achievement.
The recommendation urges society to identify children with special talents and to train them intensively from an early age.

Early cultivation of talent can be valuable in the right circumstances, but as a general policy the recommendation carries serious risks, and whether it helps or harms depends entirely on how it is carried out.
In certain fields, early and intensive training is genuinely close to necessary.
Violinists, gymnasts, and chess players who begin in childhood develop abilities that are difficult or impossible to acquire later, when the body and brain are less pliable.
Where a skill depends on years of practice during a developmental window, identifying talent early lets a child make the most of a fleeting opportunity.
Miss the window for a concert pianist or an Olympic gymnast, and no amount of later effort will fully close the gap.
A violin or a pair of figure skates placed in young hands at the right moment can quietly shape an entire life.
In these circumstances the recommendation is sound and even generous, since to delay would be to waste the very years that matter most.
However, applied broadly the policy runs into a stubborn problem: childhood talent is a poor predictor of adult achievement.
Many gifted children plateau, while many ordinary ones bloom late, so any system that sorts the young into talented and ordinary will misjudge enormous numbers of them.
Worse, the children labeled untalented may be quietly written off and denied the encouragement that might have revealed their gifts.
Labels handed out early have a way of hardening into expectations that trail a child for years.
Children develop at wildly different rates, so a snapshot taken at six tells us far less than it appears to.
A policy that picks winners at the age of six is bound to be wrong about a great many of them.

sections.role: Body — The costs of pressure and inequality

sentences.text: There is also a real cost to the children themselves and to fairness.
Intensive early training can rob a child of an ordinary childhood and impose a pressure that produces burnout rather than brilliance.
And because wealthy families can spot and fund talent far more easily, a formal program risks widening rather than narrowing the gap between rich and poor.
A childhood spent wholly in training for one pursuit can leave a person narrow, fragile, and unready for a life that rarely goes to plan.
Talent that depends on early investment will too often turn out to mean the talent that money happened to notice.
In conclusion, the recommendation is wise in some circumstances and dangerous in others.

Society should certainly nurture exceptional ability, especially where a developmental window makes early training essential, but it should do so through broad and flexible opportunity rather than rigid early selection.
Genuine talent, given broad opportunity, has a way of announcing itself in time.
The aim should be to give every child the chance to discover a talent, not to decide at six which children are permitted to have one.
